newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Congress to arbitrate Ecuador's transition process.
newsitem.headline: Congress to arbitrate Ecuador's transition process.

text.p: Ecuador's shaky transition process, with an interim president refusing to hand over power, moves back to Congress on Tuesday with a key vote to decide who should rule the small Andean nation until August 1998.
An extraordinary session of Congress at which its leader, Fabian Alarcon, has said he will be appointed president has been set for 4 p.m. (2100 GMT).
But Alarcon's plans to rule until Aug. 10, 1998, have been scuttled by interim president Rosalia Arteaga's intention to fully respect the Constitution, and not step down as expected.
If Congress appoints Alarcon on Tuesday, Ecuador "will enter a period of congressional dictatorship," she told reporters late on Monday at the ornate Carondelet presidential palace.

Arteaga, the first woman president in Ecuador's 167-year history, was appointed head of a caretaker government on Sunday in an apparent deal between lawmakers and the armed forces to solve the protracted constitutional and political crisis.

The crisis erupted on Thursday when Abdala Bucaram, a flamboyant populist whose eccentric behaviour earned him the nickname "El Loco" (the madman), was ousted by a divided Congress on grounds of "mental incompetence". The vote followed two days of paralysing strikes over harsh government austerity measures.

Arteaga, a 40-year-old lawyer and former education minister, insists neither Alarcon nor anyone else can assume the presidency until a constitutional reform is passed empowering Congress to appoint presidents.

In a brief interview with reporters, she repeated that "Congress must first reform the Constitution and then appoint a president. I am not clinging to power here because I know it's a completely transitional situation."

Stressing that the military, which proved to be the ultimate power-broker in Ecuador, "has been very respectful of the democratic institutions," she said "there is no puppet at the head of the country."
Arteaga's advisers say that without constitutional reform, which must be approved by a two-thirds majority of the 82-member Congress, legislators have no authority to name anyone president.
Parliamentary sources said Alarcon, 50, the only visible candidate to contest power to Arteaga, could find it difficult to muster the necessary votes to pass constitutional reform.
The accord paving the way for Alarcon to take over as president specified that he could be appointed by a simple majority of Congress, without any constitutional reforms.

Angered and wrong-footed by Arteaga's determination to remain in office "as long as necessary to restore democratic order," Alarcon repeated that Ecuadoreans would have to accept the verdict of Tuesday's congressional vote.
"Whether she complies with Congress decision or not ... we'll have to respect constitutional norms ... and this is good news and will allow tomorrow's vote to be positive," he told reporters.
At a news conference later, he confidently sounded as the next interim president saying "the transitional year will lay the foundations to emerge from this terrible situation."

"The relationship between legislative and the executive power will be one of cordiality," he added, in an apparent reference to Bucaram's abrasive style, which included public insults to political opponents.
Alarcon had been voted in as president on Thursday but Bucaram refused to step down until Sunday when the defence minister quit and the plan to hand over interim power to Arteaga was announced.
Bucaram announced he would start an international tour next weekend to explain why and how he was victim of what he called a military-backed "congressional coup."

Speaking to Reuters at his home in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil, he said he planned to travel to the United States and several Latin American countries, including Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Peru, Colombia and Panama.tn
He also said he would call for a nationwide march on Feb. 26 towards Quito "to reinstate the president elected by the people."
